title: GIDEON HAD SEVENTY SONS BECAUSE HE HAD MANY WIVES—Then His Concubine’s Son Nearly Wiped Them Out
paragraphs: GIDEON HAD SEVENTY SONS BECAUSE HE HAD MANY WIVES—Then His Concubine’s Son Nearly Wiped Them Out
The frightening story hidden between Gideon’s victory and Abimelech’s massacre—and the warning every Christian family needs to hear before private compromise becomes somebody else’s inheritance.
There is a sentence in the Bible that is frightening precisely because of how quietly it appears.
No thunder.
No prophet screaming judgment.
No army approaching.
Just one sentence about a famous man’s private life.
And then, one chapter later, bodies begin falling.
Gideon had survived something most people never survive.
Fear.
War.
Impossible odds.

He had watched God reduce his army until only three hundred men remained. He had heard the Midianites described as numerous as locusts. He had carried the insecurity of the man who once said his clan was the weakest and he was the least in his father’s house.
Yet God used him.
That is the Gideon many of us remember.
The fleece.
The torches.
The jars.
The trumpets.
The three hundred.
The victory.
But if you stop reading when Gideon becomes victorious, you miss one of the most disturbing lessons of his entire life.
Because sometimes the most dangerous chapter of a person's life begins after the miracle.
Sometimes we know how to depend on God when we are terrified...
but we do not know how to remain humble when we become successful.
And tucked near the end of Judges 8 is the sentence that should make every parent, leader, pastor, husband, wife, and believer slow down:
“Gideon had seventy sons of his own issue, for he had many wives.”
The Hebrew is painfully direct.
וּלְגִדְעוֹן הָיוּ שִׁבְעִים בָּנִים יֹצְאֵי יְרֵכוֹ כִּי־נָשִׁים רַבּוֹת הָיוּ לוֹ
The essential sense is unmistakable:
Gideon had seventy biological sons...
because he had many wives.
Then Scripture adds another detail.
There was also a woman in Shechem.
She was his concubine.
And she bore Gideon another son.
His name was Abimelech.
At first, that can sound like an ancient genealogical footnote.
It isn't.
It is the fuse.
Judges 8:31 records that Gideon’s concubine in Shechem bore him a son whom he named Abimelech.
And then Gideon died.
That is when the consequences he could no longer control began walking around in the bodies of his children.
Read that again.
Gideon was gone.
But Gideon’s household remained.
His victories remained.
His reputation remained.
His decisions remained.
His sons remained.
And Abimelech remained.
This is where Scripture becomes uncomfortable because it refuses to give us cardboard heroes.
The Bible does not need to erase Gideon’s victories to tell us about Gideon’s failures.
Nor should we.
God genuinely used Gideon.
God genuinely delivered Israel through him.
And Gideon nevertheless made choices whose consequences extended beyond his lifetime.
That should terrify us just enough to make us honest.
Because perhaps you have been assuming that yesterday's obedience makes today's compromise harmless.
It doesn't.
You can have a testimony and still need repentance.
You can have been mightily used by God and still have places in your life that desperately need surrender.
You can defeat Midian publicly while allowing something dangerous to grow privately.
And this is where the story turns bloody.

After Gideon died, Israel again turned toward the Baals. They forgot the LORD who had delivered them, and they failed to show covenant loyalty toward Gideon's household. Then Abimelech went directly to his mother’s relatives in Shechem.
He understood something powerful.
Blood loyalty.
Family identity.
Political resentment.
Ambition.
He asked the leaders of Shechem, essentially, which was better: seventy sons of Gideon ruling over them, or one man?
Then came the sentence designed to close the sale:
Remember...
I am your flesh and blood.
Abimelech knew exactly which wound to touch.
He presented the seventy as outsiders and himself as family.
And Shechem listened.
Money was taken from the temple of Baal-berith and given to Abimelech.
He used it to hire reckless men.
Then he went to his father's house.
Imagine the scene before you read the next sentence too quickly.
These weren't statistics.
They had names.
Faces.
Childhood memories.
They were sons who had grown up beneath the shadow of the same father.
Perhaps some had eaten together.
Perhaps some had played together.
Perhaps some had argued over things brothers argue about.
Perhaps some remembered Gideon's stories of trumpets, torches, shattered jars and Midianites fleeing through the night.
Then their brother arrived.
Not to reconcile.
Not to talk.
Not to mourn their father.
To kill them.
Judges 9 tells us that Abimelech murdered his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal, on one stone.
Seventy sons.
Almost.
Because one escaped.
Jotham.
The youngest hid himself.
One survivor.
One witness.
One voice left alive to speak.
And suddenly that seemingly insignificant sentence from the previous chapter feels much heavier:
Gideon had many wives.

This does not mean Scripture teaches a simplistic equation that polygamy mechanically caused Abimelech's murders. Abimelech was morally responsible for his own wickedness, as were the leaders of Shechem who supported him.
But Scripture deliberately places Gideon's complicated household immediately before the violent struggle that erupted among his sons.
That matters.
And we should never confuse biblical description with biblical approval.
The Bible records many things human beings did without commanding us to imitate them.

Polygamy appears repeatedly in the Old Testament, but Genesis establishes God's foundational marriage pattern with one man and one woman becoming “one flesh,” a pattern Jesus Himself returned to when teaching about marriage.
So Judges is not inviting us to admire Gideon's collection of wives.
It is showing us a broken world.
And brokenness has descendants.
That is where Gideon's story stops being ancient history.
Because you may not have seventy sons.
You may not have many wives.
You may never become a military leader.
But every one of us is building something somebody else may have to live inside.
Your children may inherit consequences from decisions they never made.
Your spouse may carry wounds produced by battles they never started.
People around you may eventually encounter the mature version of something you keep calling “small.”
A hidden addiction.
A secret relationship.
Uncontrolled anger.
Pornography.
Pride.
Bitterness.
Greed.
Emotional neglect.
Dishonesty.
Spiritual hypocrisy.
An obsession with status.
A refusal to forgive.
A private compromise nobody knows about.
We comfort ourselves with one dangerous sentence:
“It isn't hurting anybody.”
Gideon's story whispers back:
Not yet.
Sin rarely sends you an invoice on the day you purchase it.
Sometimes the bill arrives years later.
Sometimes it arrives at your children's door.
That does not mean every suffering child is being punished for a parent's particular sin. Scripture does not permit us to make that cruel assumption.
It means something simpler and more sobering:
Our choices affect other people.
And some consequences outlive us.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Because some of us know what it feels like to inherit a war.
You did not create the alcoholism in your family.
You inherited its aftermath.
You did not create your father's anger.
But you learned to flinch because of it.
You did not create your mother's wounds.
But somehow you became responsible for navigating them.
You did not choose the divorce.
The betrayal.
The abandonment.
The dysfunction.
The silence.
The secrets.
Yet you grew up among their ruins.
And now perhaps you are terrified that you will become what hurt you.
Listen carefully.
Judges 9 is not the end of the Bible.
Abimelech is not the final Son Scripture wants you looking toward.
Another Son is coming.
Not the son of Gideon.
The Son of God.
And He does something Abimelech never could.
Abimelech destroyed his brothers to obtain a throne.
Jesus left His throne to save His enemies.
Abimelech shed the blood of others to make himself king.
Jesus allowed His own blood to be shed to rescue sinners.
Abimelech's kingdom was built through death.
Christ's Kingdom brings life through His death and resurrection.
Abimelech climbed toward power over the bodies of his brothers.
Jesus descended into humiliation and gave Himself for people who had rebelled against Him.
Do you see Him?
This is why Christianity is not merely advice about becoming a slightly better version of yourself.
You need more than advice.
So do I.
We need a Savior.
Because eventually the Bible stops allowing us to blame only what our parents handed us.
Maybe you inherited wounds.
But eventually you make choices.
Maybe somebody sinned against you.
But bitterness can still become your sin.
Maybe your childhood explains why you struggle.
But explanation is not transformation.
Jesus does not merely want to help you manage the family darkness.
He came to bring you out of darkness.
Maybe your father failed.
Maybe your mother failed.
Maybe your marriage failed.
Maybe you failed your children.
Maybe you crossed lines you swore you would never cross.
Maybe the person everyone sees at church looks nothing like the person staring at your phone at 2:13 in the morning.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a secret.
And somewhere underneath all the religious language is one exhausted thought:
If people knew everything about me, would Jesus still want me?
Look at the cross.
That is your answer.
Christ did not die for an edited version of you.
He died for sinners.
Repentance does not mean pretending your past never happened.
It means turning from sin toward the One who already knows what happened.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace looks evil directly in the face, calls it what it is, and announces that the blood of Jesus is sufficient to forgive the repentant sinner.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because every broken relationship immediately repairs itself.
Not because repentance erases history.
But because history does not have to remain your master.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the previous chapters weren't written...
but by changing where the story is going.
That means your father's sin does not have to become your identity.
Your mother's brokenness does not have to become your destiny.
Your divorce does not have to become your definition.
Your addiction does not have to become your name.
Your secret does not have to become your grave.
Your family's pattern does not have to become your children's inheritance.
In Christ, cycles can end.
Not through motivational slogans.
Through repentance.
Through truth.
Through forgiveness.
Through the Holy Spirit.
Through obedience.
Through the Gospel.
Perhaps your greatest spiritual victory will never be witnessed by thousands.
Perhaps it will happen tonight when you finally confess what you have been hiding.
Perhaps it happens when you delete the number.
Close the browser.
Tell your spouse the truth.
Ask your child to forgive you.
Call the person you wounded.
Seek biblical counsel.
Return what wasn't yours.
Walk away from the affair.
Pour out the bottle.
Stop feeding the resentment.
Open the Bible again.
Get on your knees.
And whisper the prayer pride has prevented you from praying:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Because sometimes breaking a generational cycle does not look dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like one trembling person deciding:
The darkness stops with me.
Be honest.
And if Christ has already broken something that once seemed impossible to break, tell somebody.
Your testimony might become another person's evidence that chains really can fall.
Not because every sentence will feel comfortable tomorrow, but because temptation has a remarkable ability to make yesterday's conviction feel distant.
Come back when compromise starts negotiating again.
Not as a trick for an algorithm.
Think about one person scrolling tonight who is silently becoming exhausted from carrying a family pattern they don't know how to break.
One father.
One mother.
One teenager.
One struggling Christian.
One prodigal.
One person who still thinks they are too dirty to come home.
Your share could put the Gospel in front of them at exactly the moment they are finally willing to listen.
It doesn't.
They don't.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior replaces faithful giving to your local church or the other acts of generosity God may call you to.
It doesn't.
Scripture says giving should come from a heart that has decided freely, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
Pray.
Follow.
Save the teaching.
Share it publicly.
Send it privately.
Put the Gospel where somebody hurting might find it.
Because Gideon's story leaves us with a question far more personal than what happened to seventy sons thousands of years ago.
What are you building that will remain when you are gone?
What are you tolerating today that somebody you love may encounter tomorrow?
And what needs to be surrendered to Jesus while there is still time to change the inheritance?
Gideon could defeat an army.
But military victory could not redeem his household.
You cannot save yourself either.
But Jesus can save sinners.
Jesus can forgive what you confess.
Jesus can transform what you surrender.
Jesus can teach a wounded father how to become gentle.
Jesus can teach an abandoned daughter that abandonment is not her identity.

Jesus can take the addict, the adulterer, the angry, the ashamed, the religious hypocrite, the exhausted believer, the prodigal who smells like the far country—and write a chapter grace alone could have authored.
So don't merely finish this article.
Respond to Christ.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Confess what darkness has taught you to conceal.
Receive the mercy you could never earn.
And then live differently.
Because perhaps the most beautiful inheritance you can leave your children is not money.
Not property.
Not your surname.
Not even stories about everything you accomplished.
Perhaps it is the memory of a mother or father who finally became humble enough to say:
“I was wrong.”
“Jesus forgave me.”
“And by His grace, the cycle ended here.”
Tell the truth.
What cycle are you asking Jesus to end with you?
Even if all you can write is:
That is enough to remind another wounded person that they are not the only one still fighting.
Because the stone where Abimelech murdered his brothers is not the final stone in Scripture.
There was another stone.
A stone rolled across the entrance of a tomb.
And on the third day, that stone could not keep Jesus Christ inside.
Death did not get the final word.
Sin did not get the final word.
The grave did not get the final word.
And if you belong to Christ...
neither does your family's darkest chapter.
You may have inherited the ruins—but in Jesus Christ, you do not have to hand them to the next generation.
